source_text: Sed ea satis erit praecerpsisse, in quibus et ratio Baptismi recognoscitur prima illa, qua jam tunc etiam ipso habitu praenotabatur ad Baptismi figuram, Dei spiritum, qui ab initio supervectabatur super aquas, intinctos reformaturum. Sanctum autem utique super sanctum ferebatur; aut ab eo quod superferebatur, id quod ferebat, sanctitatem mutuabatur. Quoniam subjecta quaeque materia, ejus quae desuper imminet, qualitatem rapiat necesse est, maxime corporalis spiritalem, et penetrare et insidere facilem per substantiae suae subtilitatem. Ita de Sancto sanctificata natura aquarum, et ipsa sanctificare concepit. Nemo dicat: Numquid ipsis enim aquis tinguimur quae tunc in primordio fuerunt? non utique ipsis nisi ex ea parte, qua genus quidem unum, species vero complures. Quod autem generi attributum est, etiam in specie redundat. Ideoque nulla distinctio est, mari quis an stagno, flumine an fonte, lacu an alveo diluatur, nec quidquam refert inter eos quos Joannes in Jordane, et quos Petrus in Tiberi tinxit. Nisi et ille spado, quem Philippus inter vias fortuita aqua tinxit, plus salutis aut minus retulit. Igitur omnes aquae de pristina originis praerogativa sacramentum sanctificationis consequuntur, invocato Deo. Supervenit enim statim spiritus de coelis, et aquis superest, sanctificans eas de semetipso, et ita sanctificatae vim sanctificandi combibunt. Quanquam ad simplicem actum competat similitudo, ut, quoniam vice sordium delictis inquinamur, aquis abluamur. Sed delicta, sicut non in carne comparent, quia nemo super cutem portat maculam idololatriae, aut stupri, aut fraudis; ita ejusmodi in spiritu sordent, qui est auctor delicti. Spiritus enim dominatur, caro famulatur; tamen utromque inter se communicant reatum, spiritus ob imperium, caro ob ministerium. Igitur medicatis quodammodo aquis per Angeli interventum, et spiritus in aquis corporaliter diluitur, et caro in eisdem spiritaliter mundatur.
pass_a_gloss: But it will be enough to have briefly mentioned those things in which the reason of Baptism is recognized, that first one, by which even then the Spirit of God, who from the beginning was borne over the waters, was already prefigured as going to reform those who were dipped in the water, by the very fact that it was borne over holy things. For the Holy Spirit was certainly borne over what is holy; or from what it was borne over, it borrowed holiness. Since every subject matter necessarily takes on the quality of what hangs over it, especially the spiritual over the physical, and easily penetrates and dwells in it due to the subtlety of its substance. Thus, the nature of the water was sanctified by the Holy One, and it itself began to sanctify. Let no one say: Are we indeed baptized in the very waters that were there in the beginning? Not, of course, in those very waters, except insofar as the genus is one, but the species are many. But what is attributed to the genus also overflows into the species. And so, there is no distinction whether one is baptized in the sea or in a pool, in a river or in a spring, in a lake or in a basin, nor does it matter between those whom John baptized in the Jordan and those whom Peter baptized in the Tiber. Unless also that eunuch, whom Philip baptized with chance water on the road, received more or less salvation. Therefore, all waters, by the prerogative of their original source, attain the sacrament of sanctification, with God invoked. For the Spirit immediately comes from heaven and remains with the waters, sanctifying them from itself, and thus the sanctified waters will imbibe the power of sanctifying. Although the likeness is suited to a simple act, so that, just as we are defiled by sins, we are washed with water. But sins do not appear in the flesh, because no one carries the stain of idolatry or adultery or fraud on their skin; rather, such things defile the spirit, which is the author of sin. For the spirit dominates, the flesh serves; yet both communicate guilt to each other, the spirit due to its command, the flesh due to its ministry. Therefore, with the waters somehow healed through the intervention of the Angel, and the spirit is corporally washed away in the waters, and the flesh is spiritually cleansed in them.

pass_b_english: I've said enough on the points where the logic of Baptism first surfaces—points that already foreshadowed, by the mere fact of the Spirit's presence, how the Spirit of God, who hovered over the waters at creation, would one day reform those who are dipped. The Holy Spirit was certainly borne over what is holy, and it borrowed holiness from the holy element it hovered above. Because any underlying matter inevitably takes on the quality of what hangs over it—especially when the spiritual overshadows the physical—and because the spiritual easily penetrates and dwells in the physical through the subtlety of its substance, the nature of the waters was sanctified by the Holy One and thereby gained the power to sanctify in turn. No one should ask: Are we actually baptized in the very same waters that existed at the beginning? Of course not in those identical waters, except insofar as the genus is one while the species are many; whatever belongs to the genus also overflows into every species. Consequently, it makes no difference whether someone is washed in the sea or a pool, a river or a spring, a lake or a basin, nor does it matter between those John baptized in the Jordan and those Peter baptized in the Tiber—unless you think the eunuch Philip baptized with chance water on the road received more or less salvation. Therefore, all waters, by the prerogative of their original source, obtain the sacrament of sanctification once God is invoked. For the Spirit immediately comes from heaven and remains upon the waters, sanctifying them from itself, and these sanctified waters then imbibe the very power to sanctify. Admittedly, the analogy fits a simple act: just as we are defiled by sins, we are washed with water. But sins do not show up on the flesh, because no one carries the stain of idolatry, adultery, or fraud on their skin; rather, such things defile the spirit, which is the author of sin. The spirit dominates, the flesh serves; yet both share the guilt—the spirit because it commands, the flesh because it executes. So, with the waters somehow healed through the Angel's intervention, the spirit is corporally washed in the waters while the flesh is spiritually cleansed in them.
